subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage:
First of the month. Indu received two hundred rupees and set three jars on the shelf. "One for a treat, one for the book I want, one for giving," she said. Eighty into the first, ninety into the second, thirty into the third.
Second Saturday. She took twenty from the treat jar for jalebis. Her cousin Vishal had lost his lunch money, so she dropped ten rupees from the giving jar into his hand.
Last day. The book jar held ninety, and the book cost more. Indu shrugged. Next month it would fit.

qa.q: How many jars did Indu use?
What was Indu feeling as she saw the book jar was still short?
qa.a: Calm and patient, since she shrugged and knew it would fit the next month.

qa.q: What could Indu do if she wants the book sooner, and why?
qa.a: She could take a little more from the treat jar for a month or earn a few rupees with small jobs at home, so the book jar fills faster.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Indu gave him the ten rupees?
qa.a: Grateful and relieved, since he had lost his lunch money.

grounding: A girl splits her monthly money into three jars for a treat, a book she wants and giving, and uses each for its purpose.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage: Jasleen, you keep asking why this old tea tin has three lids. Sit. When I was ten, my mother began giving me two hundred rupees on the first of each month. The first month I spent all of it on sweets by the fifth day, then cried when the bookshop got the bird book I wanted. So I sat on the back step and argued with myself. "If I buy nothing, I'm miserable. If I buy everything, I'm miserable later." I found three tins. One for treats now, one for the bird book, and one small one for giving: the temple box, or my friend Dawa, whose father was out of work. Every month I, Pema, thought again about how much went where. That is why the lids are three.

qa.q: How much money did Pema's mother give on the first of each month?
What was Pema feeling while arguing on the back step?
qa.a: Pema felt torn: buying nothing seemed miserable, but spending everything had already left Pema miserable when the bird book came.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Setting up three separate tins, because it turned one big temptation each month into a small, visible split that could be rethought every month.

qa.q: How might Dawa have been affected by the giving tin?
qa.a: Dawa, whose father was out of work, may have felt cared for, though perhaps a little awkward about receiving help from a friend.

grounding: An elder recalls dividing monthly pocket money into tins for treats, saving and giving, reasoning it through as a child.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage: The two hundred rupees came late this month, on the fifteenth, and the school fair was only two days away. Madhuri spread the notes on her bed while her little brother Vijay watched. "If I take it all to the fair, the storybook I'm saving for moves further away," she said aloud. "But if I take nothing, I'll just stand there watching everyone eat." She folded a hundred into the jar marked FAIR. Seventy went into the jar with the book's picture taped on it. She held the last thirty for a long moment. "Class is collecting for Ritesh's family after the flood," she told Vijay. "Thirty is small, but it's something." Vijay nodded seriously and dropped his own five-rupee coin into that jar.

qa.q: When did the money come this month?
qa.a: On the fifteenth, only two days before the school fair.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhuri felt unsure about the last thirty rupees?
qa.a: She held it for a long moment, showing she felt torn between keeping it and giving it, before deciding that a small amount still helps.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri do if the fair jar feels too tight this month?
qa.a: She could talk it over with a parent and move a little between jars just this once, since the split is her own plan to adjust, not a fixed rule.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to see his sister's plan?
qa.a: He watches seriously and adds his own coin, so the giving jar seems to inspire him to join in. 🙂

grounding: A girl thinks aloud as she splits her late monthly money into jars for the fair, a book and a class collection.
